video_title: The Fed Is A Sideshow While The AI Trade Implodes | Weekly Roundup
gist: Forward Guidance weekly roundup: the hosts call the Fed's hold (with Hammack and Cook dissents) a sideshow and argue the real story is the AI trade fracturing after Microsoft ($38B vs $45B est.) and Google ($51B vs $55B est.) guided capex below estimates, while credit spreads widen, real rates sit at 20+ year highs and an oil supply crisis threatens growth. Quinn argues commodity-style bubbles take as long to unwind as they took to inflate, expects post-midterm escalation to force oil higher, sees gold (below $3,900) bleeding on sovereign liquidity selling, and views the $6B Binance hack as a bottom-ish but prolonging signal for crypto.

themes.theme: Fed as sideshow, hawkish single-mandate CBs

insights.claim: The Fed held rates as fully priced, with two dissents (Hammack and Cook, reportedly Cook's first ever), and upgraded its activity language from expanding at a 'solid pace' to a 'strong pace'.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Statement tilts hawkish on growth even as forward indicators weaken.
insights.quote: they upgraded the activity expanding from solid pace to strong pace

insights.claim: Quinn calls it the most meaningless Fed meeting in a long time, arguing the Fed is handcuffed because hiking would throw gasoline on a precarious situation in AI, commodity supply shortages and soon growth, and he thinks a December move comes off the table.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Don't trade the Fed; trade AI, energy and growth.
insights.quote: I think the Fed is sort of a sideshow at this stage.

insights.claim: Quinn expects the November CPI print to show a fourth straight month of accelerating inflation.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Stagflationary setup with the Fed unwilling to respond.
insights.quote: I think that'll be the fourth straight month of accelerating inflation.

insights.claim: The Fed chair announced that next year one of eight meetings will become a non-live strategy meeting, and the following year meetings drop to six with two focused on strategy; the legal minimum is four.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Fewer live meetings reduces market focus on Fed guidance.

insights.claim: Quinn interprets fewer FOMC meetings as consistent with enabling financial repression: running too-easy policy, monetizing debt, then 'stepping aside' when inflation arrives.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Structural setup for persistent negative real returns on cash/bonds.

insights.claim: The ECB has been hiking and Christine Lagarde plans to leave early in February; Europe still has about three hikes priced, which the hosts call 'insane' for an energy importer.
insights.speaker: Co-host / Quinn
insights.so_what: European hikes into an energy shock lock in a growth slowdown.

insights.claim: Quinn says Europe historically hikes into energy shocks every 10–20 years and reverses about a year later.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Positions for eventual ECB reversal (front-end European rates).

insights.claim: The Bank of Canada hiked and signaled more despite two consecutive sharply negative jobs reports (with downward revisions) and flatlining GDP; the co-host attributes it to single-mandate reaction to oil-driven inflation and defending CAD against a rallying dollar.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Single-mandate central banks are tightening into weakness to defend currencies.

insights.claim: Quinn expects the dollar to peak and roll over once markets recognize the emptiness of Fed promises and that the AI unwind and oil-driven demand hit force the Fed to be more accommodative than inflation warrants, though it could take a week to three months.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Dollar strength is late-cycle; position for reversal over months.

insights.claim: Microsoft guided capex of $38 billion versus $45 billion estimates and Google $51 billion versus $55 billion, the first hyperscaler capex guides below estimates, which the co-host had long flagged as the 'show's over' signal.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Top of the AI capex pyramid is decelerating; downstream suppliers face an air pocket.
insights.quote: Microsoft, yeah, they they're saying 38 billion versus estimates of 45 billion.

insights.claim: The co-host says Google search revenue is plummeting due to AI and changing consumer habits.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: AI is cannibalizing Google's core business while it also cuts capex.

insights.claim: Computer equipment investment is the largest GDP contribution since 1959, and AI buildout has been the main source of real GDP growth, partly offset in GDP math by semiconductor imports from Korea and Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: A capex slowdown translates directly into a U.S. growth slowdown.
insights.quote: computer equipment investment is the largest GDP contribution since 1959

insights.claim: The co-host argues GDP data is backward-looking while forward capex estimates are slowing, alongside foreign hikes and an energy crisis, implying at minimum a growth slowdown.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Expect growth disappointments to follow capex misses.

insights.claim: Quinn says over the last 3–6 months real rates have risen to levels as high or higher than the GFC (20+ year highs) and credit spreads have widened dramatically, especially for AI/hyperscaler capex spenders whose falling cash flow has made them reliant on debt and equity issuance.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Rising cost of capital lowers the return on AI capex and forces cuts.

insights.claim: Quinn calls the AI trade possibly the largest leveraged bubble in history, citing 3x semiconductor ETFs (SOXL) with about a third of a trillion notional and a $45 billion hedge fund levered four times, now being unwound one by one.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Leverage unwinds amplify downside as they did upside.

insights.claim: Quinn argues hyperscalers cannot smoothly 'land the plane' after overspending tens to hundreds of billions above sustainable levels, and must slam on the brakes.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Capex cuts may be sharper than consensus models assume.

insights.claim: Quinn's framework: in cyclical commodity industries (semis, oil and gas, crypto) the time to rinse out excesses usually equals the time the bubble took to inflate.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-year bear market in AI hardware, not a quick dip.
insights.quote: the time it takes to rinse it out is usually equal to the to the amount of time that the bubble was being blown

insights.claim: Drawing on oil and gas experience, Quinn explains that levered producers keep producing as prices fall to cover fixed interest costs, prolonging supply gluts; he applies this to neoclouds and chip producers with debt-funded data centers.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Compute oversupply and price pressure could persist even as demand slows.
insights.quote: it prolongs the supply glut basically

insights.claim: The co-host says the credit window has effectively closed for neoclouds, leaving dilutive equity issuance as their main financing leg.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Equity holders of neoclouds face dilution risk.
insights.quote: try to issue some corporate bonds if you're if you're NeoCloud. Like good luck

insights.claim: The co-host notes the July memory-trade blowup was a leverage washout while hyperscalers were still beating capex estimates, whereas prices are now back at those lows on a fundamental story; Intel fell 28% in a day.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Current weakness is fundamental, not just positioning, making it more durable.

insights.claim: Quinn says the most bearish thing for AI investors is bulls calling compute 'the next traded commodity', since commoditization means margins go to zero, a dynamic already visible with open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Commoditized compute erodes pricing power across the stack.

insights.claim: The co-host separates AI's consumer surplus (his own token usage up ~10x in months) from its financing economics, citing the late-1990s telecom buildout where cable builders went bankrupt while later companies captured the value.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: One can be a technology bull and an AI-infrastructure equity bear.

insights.claim: The co-host says Anthropic's S-1 shows an improving business with a technical net loss driven by convertible note markups, but notes the need to train a new frontier model every few months versus commoditization of average tasks.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab economics look better than feared but face open-model pressure.

insights.claim: Quinn says he is not at the buying point for semiconductors yet and jokes his first bullish semis call may come in 2027.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Stay bearish/flat on semis near term.

insights.claim: Quinn says oil has risen straight up for two to three months barely touching its daily trend even during a period of peace ahead of the midterms, while futures positioning is falling and volume is low — few people are long.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Under-owned, trending asset with a catalyst ahead.
insights.quote: I don't know anyone's long this thing

insights.claim: Quinn argues the supply disruption is so large that the U.S. must act to unblock it, making escalation mandatory after the midterms; without it oil is a 'one-way train higher', and the view that oil could revert to $60 at any time is the wrong framing.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: He advocates long oil via early-2027 expiries.
insights.quote: The supply problem is so great, they need to actually do something about it

insights.claim: The co-host floats that oil could go to $150 in a record energy supply crisis, which the Fed cannot acknowledge yet.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Tail scenario for energy and growth.

insights.claim: Quinn says natural gas in Europe and Asia costs about 11 times the U.S. price for the same molecule (China lower), making European reshoring, defense, shipbuilding and munitions production uncompetitive.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Structural competitiveness gap favors U.S. industry over Europe.
insights.quote: 11 times the cost of natural gas

insights.claim: Gold set a new roughly one-year low below $3,900 despite falling nominal yields and net dovish rhetoric, contrary to the usual real-rate relationship.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Gold is trading on liquidity, not rates.

insights.claim: Quinn attributes gold's weakness to energy-short nations and central banks selling reserves built up over the past two to three years to defend currencies amid a liquidity crunch, alongside rising cross-asset correlations as everyone sells what they can.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Gold remains fundamentally sound but faces forced selling near term.
insights.quote: Hey, sell what you can because there's some stuff we got to cover here.

insights.claim: Quinn's gold trading rule: price is now below the summer lows, so he would only care again if it recovers those lows, regains moving averages and catalysts/positioning align; until then step aside.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Clear invalidation level: summer lows.

insights.claim: Quinn argues inflation is an invisible tax people cannot quantify but feel, manifesting as frustration, blame and civil unrest, linking viral U.S. affordability stories, Paris riots and the French bond spread over Bunds/BTPs.
insights.speaker: Quinn / Co-host
insights.so_what: Political and sovereign-spread risk rise together in inflationary cycles.
insights.quote: inflation is this invisible tax that you can't see

insights.claim: Quinn expects the House to be 'a blood bath' for Republicans while the Senate map favors them, yielding a split Congress either way, with winning Republicans pushed toward populist, anti-data-center and anti-AI positions.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Bipartisan anti-data-center politics is a regulatory headwind for AI buildout.

insights.claim: Quinn notes governors who were strongly pro-data center six months ago are now talking about pauses and moratoriums.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Local permitting risk for AI infrastructure is rising.

insights.claim: The co-host cautions that prediction markets priced Brazil's incumbent at ~80% and he lost, so a Democratic sweep priced as base case is not a given.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Avoid over-trusting prediction-market odds.

insights.claim: A roughly $6 billion hack hit Binance; Circle and Tether froze funds such that almost $3 billion may be recovered and Binance said it will cover the rest.
insights.speaker: Co-host
insights.so_what: Contained financially but damages newcomer sentiment.

insights.claim: The hosts see the hack as more of a bottom signal than a top but expect it to prolong consolidation, with Quinn's base case that crypto conditions are not fertile until sometime next year.
insights.speaker: Quinn / Co-host
insights.so_what: Patience over aggressive crypto re-entry.
insights.quote: it is more of a bottomy signal than a top one

insights.claim: Quinn argues gold needs to bottom before Bitcoin can stabilize, since both rallied on the same monetary-intervention drivers, and gold's full retracement to new lows could be ominous for Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Quinn
insights.so_what: Watch gold as a leading indicator for Bitcoin.
insights.quote: I think you have to see analog gold bottom before you're going to get their ability on the crypto.
